text: The QFT circuit from last lesson uses O of n squared gates to perform the same transform the classical FFT does in O of N log N operations, where N equals 2 to the n. That sounds like a straightforward exponential win. It is real — and it is also not the free lunch it sounds like. This lesson is the honesty check that makes the rest of this chapter's algorithms make sense.

Stated precisely: the classical FFT transforms N numbers in O of N log N, which is O of n times 2 to the n, arithmetic operations. The QFT circuit transforms the same size amplitude vector using O of n squared quantum gates. Comparing those gate counts for the same-size transform really is an exponential improvement in n, and that part is correct and not in dispute — building the transform itself is exponentially cheaper, gate for gate, on a quantum computer.

Here's the catch. A classical FFT hands you the explicit list of all N output values — print them, store them, use them however you want. A quantum state isn't like that. After running the QFT circuit, a single measurement collapses the register to exactly one basis state, sampled by probability, and every other amplitude's information is simply gone. Reconstructing the full output vector the way a classical FFT would requires re-running the whole circuit and re-measuring many times — and done honestly, that erodes or eliminates the gate-count advantage.

This isn't a flaw, it's a scoping condition: the QFT's exponential speedup only matters when the surrounding algorithm doesn't need the full output vector, just one specific extractable fact. That's exactly how phase estimation and Shor's algorithm are built — phase estimation concentrates the register's amplitude onto, or very near, a single basis state that encodes one unknown phase, and Shor's algorithm's period-finding step is engineered so the QFT peaks the measurement probability on states that reveal the period. In both cases the exponential speedup is real precisely because the algorithm was designed in advance to need one answer, not a full readout.
Next lesson stops taking the circuit's correctness on faith: a full hand-trace of the 2-qubit QFT circuit, gate by gate, verified against Lesson 6's exact numbers.
